column1: Why use Query Store instead of relying only on cached-plan statistics?
column2:
It retains query and plan performance history across cache eviction.
Cache eviction removes a compiled plan and its cache-based totals. Query Store keeps its captured plans and runtime summaries in the database, so you can compare earlier performance within its retention limits.
Review source

column1: How does Query Store group runtime statistics for repeated executions of a query plan?
column2:
Aggregates per plan over configurable time intervals.
Query Store groups executions of each plan into time buckets. A bucket contains summaries such as execution count and average duration rather than a row for each individual run.
Review source

column1: Which SSMS Query Store report identifies queries whose performance worsened between time periods?
column2:
Regressed Queries.
A regression is a change for the worse. Compare the earlier and later time windows to see which metric worsened and whether a different plan coincided with the change.
Review source

column1: Which SSMS Query Store report finds the largest consumers of a selected resource over a time range?
column2:
Top Resource Consuming Queries.
Choose the metric for the problem, such as CPU, and decide whether to rank by total or average. A frequently run query can rank high by total and low by average.
Review source

column1: Which SSMS Query Store report highlights inconsistent query performance?
column2:
Queries With High Variation.
High variation means the same query performs very differently across executions. Different parameter values can explain that pattern, but plan changes and resource waits can also contribute.
Review source

column1: How can Query Store plan forcing help when a new plan makes a query slower?
column2:
Restore a previously good plan while investigating the root cause.
Forcing asks the optimizer to reproduce a plan that previously performed well. This can restore acceptable performance while you investigate the regression. Keep measuring because the same plan can become less suitable as data changes.
Review source

column1: What happens if Query Store cannot force a selected plan?
column2:
The optimizer optimizes the query normally.
The optimizer compiles a plan normally if it cannot apply the forcing request. For example, an index referenced by the forced plan can be missing. Inspect forcing failures rather than assuming the flag means success.
Review source

column1: Which Query Store feature applies query hints without changing application SQL?
column2:
Query Store hints.
A Query Store hint is attached to the captured query ID. You can apply an option such as MAXDOP without changing the submitted SQL. Product support starts at SQL Server 2022 and includes supported Azure and Fabric SQL products.
Review source

column1: Which SQL Server hints take precedence over hints written in the query text or supplied by a plan guide?
column2:
Query Store hints.
The hint defined in Query Store takes precedence over a hint in the statement or plan guide. It persists across restarts and failovers, so remove or revise it when it is no longer appropriate.
Review source

column1: What tradeoff does a Query Store RECOMPILE hint make?
column2:
A new plan for each execution at the cost of compilation CPU.
Recompiling lets the optimizer use the current parameter values rather than reuse an unsuitable plan. It also spends CPU compiling every time. Query Store ignores RECOMPILE when forced parameterization applies.
Review source

column1: What happens to an incompatible Query Store tuning hint that would prevent a valid plan?
column2:
The engine ignores the hint and allows the query to execute.
An incompatible hint does not need to prevent the statement from running. The engine can disregard it and report a failure in sys.query_store_query_hints. Inspect that view before judging the effect of the hint.
Review source

column1: Which SSMS report links historical query waits to resource categories?
column2:
Query Wait Statistics.
The report groups related waits into categories by query and time period. For example, Lock points to lock waits rather than time spent on CPU. Use that category to narrow the investigation.
Review source

column1: What does a high Lock wait total in Query Store tell you about the measured query?
column2:
It spends time waiting for locks.
High Lock waits show that the query was blocked while it needed a lock. They do not identify which transaction held it. Trace live blocking or use other captured evidence to find the blocker.
Review source

column1: Which Azure portal feature visualizes Query Store resource-consumption history for Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Query Performance Insight (QPI).
Query Performance Insight is an Azure portal view for Azure SQL Database. It uses Query Store history to show resource use and trends for selected queries. An empty history cannot produce useful charts.
Review source

column1: Why might the queries visible in Query Performance Insight account for only a small share of total database resource use?
column2:
It displays only the selected top 5 to 20 queries.
The portal chart ranks a limited set of individual queries. Many smaller queries can use substantial resources together without any one of them making that list. Use Query Store views to inspect more of the workload.
Review source

column1: Which catalog view shows Query Store's actual state, requested state, and storage usage?
column2:
sys.database_query_store_options.
The desired state shows the requested mode, and the actual state shows what the engine is doing. If the two differ, review the storage usage and readonly_reason to find the cause.
Review source

column1: How do you restore Query Store collection after its storage quota is reached in Azure SQL Database?
column2:
Increase its quota or remove unneeded history, then restore READ_WRITE mode.
When the storage limit stops collection, free space or raise the limit and return Query Store to READ_WRITE. First inspect readonly_reason, because a different cause needs a different remedy.
Review source

column1: What does Query Store's AUTO capture mode prioritize?
column2:
Queries selected by execution frequency and resource consumption.
AUTO uses execution frequency and resource use to decide which queries to capture. This can omit infrequent, low-cost statements and preserve space for more useful performance history.
Review source

column1: What does Query Store's automatic size-based cleanup do?
column2:
Removes less expensive and older queries as storage approaches its quota.
Size-based cleanup frees storage when Query Store gets close to its limit. It can remove older, less expensive queries even before a time-based retention rule removes them.
Review source

column1: How do you combine Query Store average durations from intervals with different execution counts?
column2:
Weight each interval's average duration by its execution count.
An interval with 100 runs must contribute more to the overall average than an interval with one run. Multiply each average by its execution count, sum the results, then divide by the total executions.
Review source

column1: Why can filtering Query Store summaries by last_execution_time include executions older than the cutoff?
column2:
Each matching row aggregates an interval that can cross the cutoff.
last_execution_time is the latest execution in an aggregate row. If that execution meets the cutoff, the row can still include earlier executions outside the window. Query Store does not expose each run in that summary.
Review source
